title: 2 Kings 20:1–11
context: In those days Hezekiah becomes mortally ill, and Isaiah tells him to set his house in order, for he will die and not live. Hezekiah turns his face to the wall, prays, and weeps bitterly, and before Isaiah has left the middle part of the city, the LORD sends him back with the word that he has heard the prayer, seen the tears, and will add fifteen years to Hezekiah’s life and deliver the city. A cake of figs is laid on the boil, and at Hezekiah’s request the LORD gives a sign by bringing the shadow back ten steps on what the WEB calls the sundial of Ahaz, a phrase that can also be understood as the steps or stairway of Ahaz. The parallel accounts are Isaiah 38 and 2 Chronicles 32:24. Classical Arminian and Reformed readers generally affirm both God’s exhaustive foreknowledge and the reality of answered prayer, so they read the passage as largely shared ground that God works through prayer, while they describe differently how such responses relate to his eternal purpose. Those differences are already treated at Exodus 32:14, Jonah 3:10, and Joshua 10:14, and the parallel narrative is discussed in the existing boxes at Isaiah 38.

verses.text: In those days Hezekiah was sick and dying. Isaiah the prophet the son of Amoz came to him, and said to him, “The LORD says, ‘Set your house in order; for you will die, and not live.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Isaiah telling the sick Hezekiah to set his house in order, for he will die. The word is a real announcement of what is coming apart from God’s mercy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the announcement as a true word that also serves as a means to draw Hezekiah to prayer. Readers in both traditions commonly affirm that God knew the outcome from the beginning.

verses.text: Then he turned his face to the wall, and prayed to the LORD, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Hezekiah turning his face to the wall and praying. In his deepest need he turns privately and directly to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see his prayer as the response God intended to call forth. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a model of turning to God in personal crisis.

verses.text: “Remember now, LORD, I beg you, how I have walked before you in truth and with a perfect heart, and have done that which is good in your sight.” And Hezekiah wept bitterly.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Hezekiah asking the LORD to remember his faithfulness and weeping bitterly. His plea is honest and heartfelt.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see his appeal to a life lived before God in truth, not as earning favor but as a plea from a sincere heart. Readers in both traditions commonly read his tears with compassion.

verses.text: Before Isaiah had gone out into the middle part of the city, the LORD’s word came to him, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD’s word coming to Isaiah before he leaves the middle of the city. God answers swiftly and with compassion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the speed of the answer as showing God’s readiness to hear his people. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a striking turn in the story.

verses.text: “Turn back, and tell Hezekiah the prince of my people, ‘The LORD, the God of David your father, says, “I have heard your prayer. I have seen your tears. Behold, I will heal you. On the third day, you will go up to the LORD’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD saying he has heard the prayer, seen the tears, and will heal Hezekiah. They commonly stress that God genuinely responds to prayer within his relationship with his people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same words as God bringing about through prayer what he had purposed. Readers in both traditions commonly affirm God’s foreknowledge and the reality of answered prayer, differing mainly in how they relate the two.

verses.text: I will add to your days fifteen years. I will deliver you and this city out of the hand of the king of Assyria. I will defend this city for my own sake, and for my servant David’s sake.” ’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD adding fifteen years to Hezekiah’s life and promising to defend the city. Mercy extends beyond the king to his people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the promise as rooted in God’s commitment for his own sake and David’s sake. Both traditions commonly read the verse as showing God’s faithfulness to his covenant.

verses.text: Isaiah said, “Take a cake of figs.” They took and laid it on the boil, and he recovered.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Isaiah directing that a cake of figs be laid on the boil, and Hezekiah recovering. God uses ordinary means alongside his word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the figs as a means God ordains, not a substitute for his power. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as honoring both prayer and practical care.

verses.text: Hezekiah said to Isaiah, “What will be the sign that the LORD will heal me, and that I will go up to the LORD’s house the third day?”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Hezekiah asking for a sign that the LORD will heal him. His request for confirmation is not rebuked by the prophet.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the request as a desire for confirmation that God graciously grants. Both traditions commonly read the verse as showing God’s patience with human weakness.

verses.text: Isaiah said, “This will be the sign to you from the LORD, that the LORD will do the thing that he has spoken: should the shadow go forward ten steps, or go back ten steps?”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Isaiah offering Hezekiah a choice about whether the shadow should go forward or back ten steps. God gives a clear sign.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the sign as a confirmation that the LORD will do what he has spoken. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse without pressing symbolic meaning onto the shadow.

verses.text: Hezekiah answered, “It is a light thing for the shadow to go forward ten steps. No, but let the shadow return backward ten steps.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Hezekiah choosing the harder sign, that the shadow go back. He asks for something only God could do.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see his choice as seeking an unmistakable sign of God’s power. Both traditions commonly read the verse as part of the narrative rather than as a model for seeking signs.

verses.text: Isaiah the prophet cried to the LORD; and he brought the shadow ten steps backward, by which it had gone down on the sundial of Ahaz.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Isaiah crying to the LORD and the shadow going back ten steps. God confirms his word through a sign.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the sign as God’s power over his creation. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as the text presents it, without speculating about how the sign occurred.
